clue.text: Moved suddenly, seconds before crash

parts.note: a prang is British slang for a minor car crash

explanation.surface: Someone leapt into action just seconds before a collision.
explanation.definitionFit: To spring is to leap or move with a sudden jump, and the past tense keeps the sense of a quick motion.

clue.text: Unknown person, comparatively odd

definitions.meaning: someone you have never met before
the comparative of an adjective meaning odd or peculiar

explanation.definitionFit: One word serves as a noun for an unfamiliar person and as the comparative form of 'strange', meaning odder.

clue.text: Creature providing ingredients for edible stew

indicators.note: the letters of the creature are treated as the ingredients mixed together to make the words that follow

parts.note: taken as written
taken as written

explanation.surface: Some animal is being described as the source of meat for a tasty stew.
explanation.walkthrough: 'ingredients for' reads as if the creature goes into the stew, but it means its letters are what the following words are rearranged from.
explanation.definitionFit: A gnu is an African antelope, a creature in the most general sense of an animal.

clue.text: Outlaw eating right health food?

indicators.note: one piece eating another means it swallows it, so the second goes inside the first

parts.note: to outlaw something is to ban it

explanation.surface: A criminal on the run is tucking into some wholesome fare.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Outlaw' looks like a noun for a bandit but works as a verb meaning prohibit.
explanation.definitionFit: Cereal husk fibre is sold as a wholesome breakfast item, hence the question mark for a food by example.

clue.text: Very smart girl in cathedral city

parts.note: chic means stylish, very smart in dress
Hester is a girl's name

explanation.surface: A fashionable young woman is found in a city with a cathedral.
explanation.walkthrough: CHICHESTER is a city in West Sussex, England, with a medieval cathedral.
explanation.definitionFit: The West Sussex city is the seat of a bishop and has a famous Norman cathedral, so it is a cathedral city.

clue.text: Some programmes about a famous novel

indicators.note: about signals that the extracted letters are turned round
some of the word means only a part of its letters are used

explanation.surface: Several television programmes deal with a well-known work of fiction.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Some' takes AMME from inside 'programmes', and 'about' turns those letters round.
explanation.definitionFit: Jane Austen's novel of 1815 about a matchmaking heroine is among the most famous in English.

clue.text: A bit of needlework Tweedledum and Tweedledee started as well

annotationWithheld.why: Clue as held 'A bit of needlework Tweedledum and Tweedledee started as well (6)': TT (starts) + TOO gives only five letters; the A must come from the definition's 'A', so it does two jobs, and nothing signals its placing between the Ts.
annotationWithheld.clue: A bit of needlework Tweedledum and Tweedledee started as well

clue.text: I'm about to get money for betting slips

indicators.note: about means the letters of the preceding word are turned round

parts.note: taken as the letters of I'm without the apostrophe
stakes are the sums wagered on a bet

explanation.surface: A punter is about to collect money on their betting slips.
explanation.walkthrough: 'slips' looks like betting slips, but it is the definition meaning errors.
explanation.definitionFit: Slips as nouns are small errors or blunders, the plural sense of oversights.

clue.text: Within parish boundaries, courts with Catholic church leader

indicators.note: within the boundaries means the other pieces sit between the outer letters
the boundaries of a word are its first and last letters

parts.note: atria are open courts or halls in Roman houses
RC stands for Roman Catholic

explanation.surface: Inside a parish, the courtyards of a Catholic church head are described.
explanation.walkthrough: 'courts' looks like a verb for wooing, but it is a noun for open halls; 'boundaries' takes P and H from 'parish', and 'Within' puts the other pieces between them.
explanation.definitionFit: A patriarch is a senior bishop in the Orthodox and some Catholic churches, a top church leader.

clue.text: I injure back in US city

indicators.note: back means the whole run of letters is read in the reverse direction

parts.note: to maim is to injure badly

explanation.surface: Someone confesses to hurting their back while in an American city.
explanation.walkthrough: 'back' looks like the body part that is hurt, but it reverses I MAIM.
explanation.definitionFit: Miami is a major city in Florida, United States.

clue.text: Freedom of action in desert

definitions.meaning: lack of restraint or inhibition, as in doing something with wild freedom
to leave someone or something behind for good

explanation.definitionFit: One word is a noun for uninhibited freedom and a verb meaning to forsake or leave behind.

clue.text: It appears after youngster traps a bird

indicators.note: the word It is placed after the rest of the wordplay
one piece trapping another holds it inside

parts.note: a colt is a young male horse, or a young inexperienced player
taken as written

explanation.surface: A creature shows up after a young one sets a snare for a bird.
explanation.walkthrough: A COAL TIT is a small European bird of the tit family.
explanation.definitionFit: The coal tit is a small black-capped songbird of Europe and Asia.

clue.text: Carriage going back and forth

indicators.note: the word reads the same backwards and forwards, so it goes both ways

parts.note: these definition words give the whole answer, and the answer is itself the palindrome: it reads the same from either end

explanation.surface: A horse-drawn vehicle travels to and fro.
explanation.walkthrough: 'going back and forth' describes a carriage's travel but signals a word that reads the same in both directions.
explanation.definitionFit: A gig is a light two-wheeled carriage pulled by one horse.

clue.text: Animal to stand for newspaper man

parts.note: a beaver is an animal
to stand something is to tolerate or brook it

explanation.surface: Someone stands in as an animal for a man who works on a paper.
explanation.walkthrough: Lord BEAVERBROOK was a Canadian-British press baron who owned the Daily Express.
explanation.definitionFit: Lord Beaverbrook was a famous newspaper proprietor, owner of the Daily Express.

clue.text: Learner extremely ironic in Peter Pan production

indicators.note: a production of a play is a new staging, so these letters are put on in a new order
the extremes of a word are its first and last letters

explanation.surface: A trainee actor gives a very ironic performance in a staging of Peter Pan.
explanation.walkthrough: 'extremely' takes I and C from 'ironic'; 'production' rearranges them with PETER PAN.
explanation.definitionFit: An apprentice is someone learning a trade under a skilled worker.

clue.text: Bribe given by leader in Hell and accepted by angel

indicators.note: one piece accepted by another is taken inside it

parts.note: an angel is a financial backer, especially of a theatre show

indicators.note: the leader of a word is its first letter

parts.note: taken as written

explanation.surface: A bribe is offered by a ringleader in Hell and taken by an angel.
explanation.walkthrough: 'angel' looks heavenly beside Hell, but it means a theatrical backer.
explanation.definitionFit: A backhander is a covert payment, British slang for a bribe.

clue.text: Small piece not completely in code

indicators.note: not completely means the word is cut short by its final letter

parts.note: a morsel is a small piece of food

explanation.surface: A tiny fragment is not fully written in a cipher.
explanation.walkthrough: MORSE is the dots-and-dashes telegraph code.
explanation.definitionFit: Morse is the telegraphic code of dots and dashes named after its inventor.

clue.text: Novel I'm to read: The Go-Between

indicators.note: novel means new, so the letters are put into a new arrangement

explanation.surface: A reader announces they will read L. P. Hartley's novel The Go-Between.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Novel' looks like the book, but it is the anagram signal; The Go-Between is a famous novel, which deepens the trick.
explanation.definitionFit: A go-between is someone who carries messages or negotiates between two parties, an intermediary.

clue.text: A bit of advice about depression

indicators.note: about means the letters of the clue piece are turned round

parts.note: a tip is a piece of advice

explanation.surface: Someone offers a small piece of guidance about feeling low.
explanation.walkthrough: 'depression' looks like low mood, but it means a hollow in the ground.
explanation.definitionFit: A pit is a hole or hollow in the ground, a physical depression.

clue.text: Traffic controllers taking care of points

parts.note: c/o, written CO, is the postal abbreviation for care of
N, E and S are compass points: north, east and south

explanation.surface: Traffic is managed by people looking after various points.
explanation.walkthrough: Traffic cones are plastic markers used to divert traffic.
explanation.definitionFit: Plastic road markers guide and redirect vehicles, so in a playful sense they control traffic.

clue.text: Poor diet seen to be most poor

indicators.note: poor here describes the letters as badly formed, so they are rearranged

explanation.surface: A bad diet seen as a sign of extreme poverty.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Poor' looks like part of the definition, which repeats 'poor', but it signals the anagram.
explanation.definitionFit: The superlative of needy means the poorest, those in the greatest want.

clue.text: One word that is silly or sensible

indicators.note: silly means the letters are arranged in a foolish new order

explanation.surface: A single word can be either foolish or wise.
explanation.walkthrough: 'silly or sensible' looks like a pair of opposites, but 'silly' signals the anagram and 'sensible' is the definition.
explanation.definitionFit: Someone down-to-earth is practical and realistic, which is to say sensible.

clue.text: Fought for room in hospital, reportedly

indicators.note: reportedly means the word is said and heard rather than spelt

parts.note: a ward is a room for patients in a hospital

explanation.surface: Patients fought over a room in hospital, according to reports.
explanation.definitionFit: To war is to fight, so the past tense means fought.

clue.text: Goddess lacking aspiration for a long time

indicators.note: aspiration is the breathy H sound, so this H is dropped

parts.note: Hera is the queen of the Greek gods

explanation.surface: A goddess has had no ambitions for ages.
explanation.walkthrough: 'aspiration' looks like ambition, but in phonetics it is the breathy H sound.
explanation.definitionFit: An era is a long period of history.

clue.text: State capital finally missing a month

indicators.note: finally missing means the letter at the end is lost

parts.note: Augusta is the capital of the US state of Maine

explanation.surface: The final part of a state capital has gone missing for a month.
explanation.walkthrough: AUGUSTA is the capital of Maine; 'finally missing a' drops its last A.
explanation.definitionFit: August is the eighth month of the year.

clue.text: Fruit found in bed after almost thirty days

indicators.note: after means the bed is placed after the shortened month
almost means the last letter of the word is dropped

parts.note: April is one of the months with thirty days
a cot is a small bed

explanation.surface: Fruit turns up in someone's bed after nearly a month.
explanation.walkthrough: 'thirty days' recalls the rhyme 'Thirty days hath September, April, June and November'.
explanation.definitionFit: An apricot is a small orange stone fruit.

clue.text: Stuff to prepare for examination

definitions.meaning: to stuff is to pack something in tightly
to study intensively just before a test

explanation.definitionFit: One verb means to pack tightly and also to study hard at the last minute before a test.

clue.text: Piano finale not determined

parts.note: P is the musical abbreviation for piano, meaning soft
a finale is an ending

explanation.surface: The end of a piano piece has not yet been decided.
explanation.definitionFit: Something pending awaits a decision, undecided and unsettled.

clue.text: Daddy following Oscar

definitions.meaning: in the NATO phonetic alphabet the code word for P comes straight after Oscar for O

explanation.definitionFit: The childish word for father is also the radio code word that follows Oscar in the NATO alphabet.

clue.text: Letter required for some games

indicators.note: the letters required are taken from within the words that follow

explanation.surface: A letter must be sent before some games can take place.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Letter' looks like a written message, but it is the last letter of the Greek alphabet.
explanation.definitionFit: Omega is the final letter of the Greek alphabet.

clue.text: Trees providing a bit of cover, certainly sheltering crowd

indicators.note: a bit of a word is just its first letter here
one piece sheltering another covers it from outside

parts.note: yes means certainly in reply
to press is to crowd, or a press is a dense crowd

explanation.surface: Some trees give a little cover, sheltering a crowd for sure.
explanation.definitionFit: Cypresses are tall evergreen conifers, a kind of tree.
